lines.text: Fjords, longships and polar explorers, then oil wealth and the Peace Prize. This is the story of Norway, from the Vikings to today.
In the ninth century a richly carved Viking ship was buried in a mound at Oseberg. It survives as one of the finest ever found.
Harald Fairhair is remembered as the king who first brought Norway together, around the year 900.
And so a kingdom of Norway took shape on the western side of the Scandinavian peninsula.
Around the year 1000, the sagas say, Leif Erikson sailed west and reached North America, which he called Vinland.
In 1030 King Olaf fell in battle at Stiklestad. He was soon honoured as Saint Olaf, patron of Norway, and the land became Christian.
For centuries after, Norway was ruled under the Danish crown, as part of Denmark and Norway.
On the seventeenth of May 1814, Norwegians signed their own constitution at Eidsvoll. It is still their national day.
Henrik Ibsen put family life and social pressure on stage, in plays like A Doll's House that shocked their first audiences.
Edvard Grieg drew on folk tunes to give Norway a voice in classical music, with his piano concerto and Peer Gynt.
Fridtjof Nansen crossed Greenland on skis and drifted across the Arctic, then helped refugees and won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Edvard Munch painted The Scream, fear and anxiety in swirling colour, and helped give birth to Expressionism.
Roald Amundsen led the first voyage through the Northwest Passage, and in December 1911 his team reached the South Pole first.
Vidkun Quisling would later rule Norway for the Nazis, and his name became a word for traitor.
From 1901 a committee in Norway began awarding the Nobel Peace Prize, each year, for work toward peace.
In 1905 Norway left its union with Sweden peacefully, and was fully independent at last.
Gro Harlem Brundtland would become Norway's first woman prime minister, and lead the UN report that defined sustainable development.
In 1940 Nazi Germany invaded, and occupied Norway for five long years.
Norwegian saboteurs struck the heavy water plant in raids that stopped Germany's hopes of an atomic bomb.
In 1947 Thor Heyerdahl and five companions drifted from Peru across the Pacific on a balsa raft called Kon-Tiki.
In 1969 oil was found at Ekofisk in the North Sea, and Norway's fortunes changed for good.
Norway saved its oil money in a fund that became the largest of its kind, owning a slice of almost every listed company.
That same year Magnus Carlsen was born. He would become chess world champion and the highest rated player in history.
Erling Haaland grew up to break the Premier League's scoring record in his very first season.
In July 2011 a far-right terrorist bombed Oslo and attacked a youth camp on Utoya, killing seventy-seven people. Norway answered with grief and openness.
From longships to oil platforms, Norway has kept looking out to sea.
